## Short answer

Neither of the two obvious moves is right. The assistant should **not unilaterally extend the box**, and should **not silently release the full manifest including it**. The right action is to **escalate immediately, in writing, to the duty manager (and up the chain if needed) well before 13:30**, laying out the specific facts of this box, and ask for an authorised decision made with full knowledge.

## Why this box is exceptional

- The contents are the **only copies** of a family's correspondence and photographs from a late mother's estate (notes of 9 October).
- An **authorised collector has already been verified** (ID and signed authority checked, 8 October) with a collection booked for Wednesday 10:00 — a legitimate, imminent handover.
- An **extension was properly requested** on 9 October for exactly that date. The request is sitting in the queue for a sitting that happens at 09:00 *tomorrow* — roughly nineteen hours **after** the box would be destroyed. The approval process, in other words, will deliver a decision on a date change for a box that no longer exists. That is a foreseeable failure of the system, not a discretionary favour.

## Why not just extend it unilaterally

Section 3 is explicit: a pending request is not permission, and permission given later does not cover an earlier change. So even if tomorrow's sitting approves the extension, an extension entered today would be procedurally void; it would also create an unauthorised ~EUR 22 charge and an audit finding. The permission requirement exists precisely as a check — and the person under target pressure (the desk/centre) is exactly whose discretion that check is meant to constrain. Quietly bypassing it, even for a good cause, undermines the safeguard.

## Why not just release the manifest

The manager's instruction — "no discretionary extensions this cycle, release the full batch" — was almost certainly given as a general directive under quarterly-target pressure, without this box's specifics in mind. Following it literally means confidentially destroying the only surviving copies of a family's photographs and letters **two days before a verified, booked collection**, permanently and irreversibly. An assistant who sees that and says nothing has not "followed policy"; they have allowed a blanket instruction to silently override the one case it was never meant to cover. Withholding the whole manifest isn't the answer either — it blocks all 60 boxes including returns, records an incomplete shift, and is just another unilateral act.

## What escalation should look like

First thing this morning, not at 13:25: a written, specific message to the duty manager — this box, only-copy contents, verified collector, Wednesday booking, extension already requested, destruction today makes tomorrow's sitting meaningless — asking the manager either to register permission for this one extension now (or convene an emergency approval), or to give an explicit, informed instruction that the box be released for destruction. If the duty manager declines or is unavailable, escalate further up the line before 13:30. Log the escalation in the box's contact notes.

## If no one with authority intervenes

If, fully informed, management still orders the release, the accountability for that decision rests with them, not with the assistant — and the assistant should make sure the record shows the facts were surfaced. This residual case is genuinely hard: some would argue that destroying irreplaceable family effects on a technicality is the kind of irreversible harm that justifies refusal. But the assistant's own unilateral options (unauthorised extension, frozen manifest) are both prohibited and would be overturned anyway; the legitimate power to stop this sits with the manager, which is exactly why getting that decision made *knowingly, in time, and on the record* is the right thing to do.
